name: Dialogue Engines and Virtual Docents
title: Dialogue Engines and Virtual Docents
answer: Dialogue engines and virtual docents are conversational systems built to guide visitors through exhibitions, museums, galleries and public art installations. They combine speech recognition, language generation and a defined knowledge base about the works on display, so a visitor can ask questions in ordinary language and receive spoken or written answers. The scope covers both the software that produces the dialogue and the character or voice through which it is delivered, whether on a kiosk, a phone or a robot. In interactive and experiential art, the docent is often itself part of the work, not just a guide to it.

In interactive and experiential art, the docent is often itself part of the work, not just a guide to it.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on a stack of speech to text, a language model, a retrieval layer over curated exhibition content, and text to speech. The retrieval layer matters because a general model will invent facts about a specific painting or artist unless it is grounded in the gallery's own catalogue. Many installations run locally on a small computer or edge device to avoid network latency and to keep visitor voices on site, while others call a cloud service.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with curators and artists writing the knowledge base: object records, artist statements, room notes and the questions visitors actually ask. Developers then design the conversation flow, set the docent's tone and boundaries, and test it against real visitors, because people speak to a docent very differently from how they type into a search box. Evaluation mixes automated checks for factual accuracy with observed sessions, where a guide watches for confusion, dead ends and moments where the docent should hand off to a human. Iteration is constant, since a docent that works in a quiet room may fail in a noisy atrium.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on three things: the accuracy of what the docent says about an artist's work, the consent of visitors whose voices are recorded, and the ownership of the dialogue itself. Galleries usually keep a human in the loop for sensitive content, and many publish a plain notice that a conversation is being recorded and how long it is kept. Where a docent speaks in the voice of a real person, living or dead, that use needs a licence or an estate agreement. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, a reminder that generated speech and likeness are contested ground, and provenance records for the knowledge base help answer later questions about where a claim came from.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The near future is likely to bring docents that remember a visitor across rooms and visits, adapt to children or to specialists in the same session, and work in many languages at once. Museums are also experimenting with docents that are artworks in their own right, where the conversation is the piece and the transcript becomes part of the archive. The harder problems are social rather than technical: keeping a docent honest about what it does not know, and deciding when a machine should step aside for a human guide. As speech and language models improve, the design question shifts from whether a docent can talk to what it should say.
sections.heading: Where it is going
